# Supplementary methods and results

## Salmon data

We compiled data for pink, chum and sockeye salmon from a large public database of Pacific salmon spawner and recruitment time series (@Greenberg-etal2026Timevarying-productivity). These populations spanned 46.37 to 66.46 degrees in latitude and from 1948 to 2024. We discarded observations prior to 1950 due to concerns about data quality, and did not include time series that did not span at least brood years 1984-2014 and with minimal missing observation (i.e., > 80% of all years) (Figures \@ref(fig:fig-s1)-\@ref(fig:fig-s3)). We further excluded time series with known substantial hatchery influence to restrict our analysis to wild salmon populations. The resulting dataset included 66 sockeye populations, 28 chum salmon populations, and 33 pink salmon populations, grouped into three (chum) or four (sockeye and pink) large marine ecosystems/regions (Table \@ref(tab:tab-1)). The most populations in a single region were West Coast sockeye (n=26) and the fewest were in the Bering Sea for pink salmon (n=4).

Unlike for other systems and species, estimates of spawner abundance for Fraser River sockeye salmon were "effective female spawners" instead of total spawners, which accounts for the at times substantial pre-spawn mortality (i.e., mortality after arrival on the spawning grounds, but before spawning) and variable egg retention in this system. Additionally, return abundance estimates for Fraser River sockeye salmon account for en route mortality (i.e., mortality after freshwater entry, but before arrival on the spawning grounds), which can be considerable in certain years. While there is likely pre-spawn and en route mortality in other systems and species it is only systematically accounted for in the Fraser. Because of this, for modeling sockeye dynamics only, we allowed regional intrinsic productivity to arise from a common normal distribution that was allowed to differ from populations in other regions. In addition, for Fraser sockeye any confounding of freshwater temperature effects on return migration on estimates of marine temperature effects (e.g., in instances where they are correlated) in our analyses are accounted for by having adult recruitment explicitly account for freshwater migration mortality.

Sockeye can rear in freshwater for a variable length of time before migrating to sea, and both sockeye and chum can mature and return to spawn at variable ages. Where possible we used brood year specific estimates of age at ocean entry and return; when this data was not available we used estimates from adjacent years, or the mean across all years if only a few years had brood year specific estimates. In some instances for chum, there were no age data available, and so we assumed a fixed four-year life cycle, following @malick2017effects who summarize research that found that assuming a fixed four year life cycle for chum introduced minimal bias into reconstructions of their population dynamics.

## Sensitivity Analyses

Our analyses made a number of simplifying assumptions about processes that are hypothesized to influence Pacific salmon dynamics. Our intent was to quantify the statistical evidence for a relatively narrow set of hypotheses with strong a-priori justification (i.e., the model/hypotheses in the main text), and to then conduct sensitivity analyses to understand the extent to which our findings are sensitive to assumptions made during the analysis.

### Alternative climate indices

Our analyses focused on coastal SST during early marine life as an index of ecological conditions during early marine life for each salmon population. This index has been repeatedly shown to correlate with pink, chum, and sockeye productivity across our study area [@mueter2002spatial; @mueter2005relationships;@malick2017effects; @malick2020time; @connors2020climate]. However, previous analyses have also shown that the NPGO, that indexes sea surface height and is associated with primary production (e.g., nutrients, salinity, and chlorophyll-a.), can be associated with salmon productivity [@malick2017effects]. To quantify the degree to which our inference about SST and pink salmon effects were confounded by other ocean basin scale processes (e.g., like those indexed by the NPGO) we repeated our analysis with the addition of the NPGO index. Specifically, we derived indices of the NPGO by averaging monthly values over the December-March period immediately prior to ocean entry, as in @mueter2002spatial and @malick2017effects and then included it as an additional covariate in either the stationary or "era" models. As with the SST index for sockeye the NPGO index was weighted by the proportion of each brood year cohort that outmigrated in each year. There was no strong positive correlation between the NPGO index and the SST or competitor covariates when all years were considered (-0.25 and 0.04 respectively). In contrast, our SST indices were moderately strongly correlated with another commonly considered ocean basin scale index, the PDO (0.4 across all years; 0.77 in the most recent time period), and so we did not consider it further in our analyses.

Stationary models that included the additional covariate indicated that the NPGO had a relatively small by typically positive relationship with productivity (Figures \@ref(fig:fig-s7)-\@ref(fig:fig-s9)), with the exception of Gulf of Alaska pink and chum where  there was no evidence of a relationship (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s8) and \@ref(fig:fig-s8)), and Bering Sea chum where there was evidence of an inverse relationship. Importantly, considering the NPGO covariate had little effect on estimates of the effects of the SST and salmon competitor covariates. In the era models, there were larger magnitudes of positive NPGO effects in the most recent time period for sockeye (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s7)), chum from more northern latitudes (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s8)), and a negative effect for West Coast pink salmon (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s9)). Overall, the spatial and temporal patterns we describe in the main text were insensitive to the simultaneous consideration of this additional covariate.

### Alternative salmon competitor indices

To evaluate the sensitivity of our inference to alternative indices of inter- and intra-specific competition we considered four alternative competitor indices, in addition to the index of total North Pacific wide pink, chum, and sockeye salmon abundance we considered in the main text. These alternatives included: (1) the combined biomass of all sockeye, chum, and pink salmon in the North Pacific [based on conversion of adult abundance to biomass used in @ruggerone2018numbers], and the North Pacific wide abundance of just (2) pink, (3) chum, or (4) sockeye. Each represents a slightly different hypothesis about the nature of competition among salmon at sea, for example, whether competition occurs among all pink, chum, and sockeye salmon, or primarily with pink salmon, or whether biomass better indexes potential competitors than abundance. In addition, analyses that only considered an index of competitors that was the same species as the focal populations were effectively just examining evidence for intra-specific competition. 

We quantified the sensitivity of our results to these alternative assumptions by substituting each alternative index for the total abundance of pink, chum and sockeye we considered as a competitor index into the stationary models described in eqn. 1-4 in the main text. The indices were calculated in the same way as the original competitor index. We found that in general, while there were subtle differences in the estimated magnitude of competitor effects (and their interaction with SST), overall when estimated effects were strong in our baseline analysis they remained of a similar magnitude and direction when considering biomass instead of abundance but were often somewhat weaker when considering just individual species competitor indices (Figures \@ref(fig:fig-s10)-\@ref(fig:fig-s12)). 

### Detrended salmon competitor indices

The pink, chum, and sockeye salmon abundance time series we considered as an index of competition among salmon at sea exhibits an increasing time trend, in addition to high frequency year-to-year variation (Figure 1b in main text; Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s13)a). As a result it is possible that other unaccounted for processes that exhibit strong positive trends over the same period (e.g., marine mammal populations, ocean heat content) may confound our interpretation of a salmon competition "effect". While the weight of evidence for the effect of competition, with especially pink salmon, on other salmon species is much stronger [@ruggerone2023diatoms] than for these other potential ecosystem changes, as a sensitivity analysis we also conducted an analysis with the temporal signal in the salmon time series removed. To do this we fit a General Additive Model to the North Pacific pink, chum, and sockeye salmon time series (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s13)b) and used the resulting residuals of the model fit as an alternative, time trend removed, competitor index (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s13)b). We then refit the stationary model (equation 1 in Main Text) with this alternative index to each of the sockeye, chum, and pink salmon spawner-recruitment datasets.

Consistent with previous analyses that have fit models of salmon productivity to detrended salmon competitor indices [e.g., @ruggerone2015productivity; @connors2020climate], statistical evidence of an inverse relationship between sockeye productivity and pink, chum and sockeye salmon abundance remained, though as expected since long term low frequency variation in the competitor time series was removed, the magnitude of predicted percentage change in recruits-per-spawner was smaller (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-s14)).

(ref:fig-s4) Sockeye posterior distribution summaries for SST and competition coefficients from the model described in the main text (equation 1). Filled points are posterior medians (points) and 95% credible intervals (horizontal lines) for the population-specific effects of SST, and pink salmon competition, and open points are estimates from a simplified model that is fit individually and independently for each population. Solid vertical lines give the posterior median for the ocean ecosystem level effects, which represent the mean effect across all populations in an ocean ecosystem. Shaded box give the 95% credibility interval for the ecosystem-level effect with dashed lines indicating zero effect.

```{r fig-s4, out.width="90%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="(ref:fig-s4)"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/sockeye_coef_catepillar_heir_indv.png")

Points are medians of posterior distributions, lines are 95% credible intervals. Effect sizes estimated from time-varying models (pre-defined break points) are indicated with diamond-shaped points and labeled by time period: "Early" (1960-1988), "Middle" (1989-2010), or "Late" (2011-2016). Estimates from stationary models considering all years are indicated with square points and labeled "All".

```{r fig-s7, out.width="90%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="(ref:fig-s7)"}

# Tables


(ref:tab-1) Population considered in our analyses, ocean region, first and last brood year (BY), and approximate ocean entry point.


```{r tab-1, tab.cap = "(ref:tab-1)"}

sk_tbl <- read.csv(here("data/sockeye/master_sockeye_stock_info.csv"))
sk_tbl$Species = "Sockeye"

ch_tbl <- read.csv(here("data/chum/master_chum_stock_info.csv"))
ch_tbl$Species = "Chum"

pk_tbl <- read.csv(here("data/pink/master_pink_stock_info.csv"))
pk_tbl$Species = "Pink"

tbl <- rbind(sk_tbl, ch_tbl, pk_tbl)

tbl_order <- tbl[,c(11,1,10,8,9,4,5)]

names(tbl_order) <-c("Species", "Population", "Ocean Region", "First BY", "Last BY", "Lat.", "Lon.")
knitr::kable(tbl_order,
             row.names = FALSE,
             align = "lrrcccc",
             booktabs = T,
             longtable=T) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"))

```


(ref:tab-2) Estimated mean effect sizes by region for SST and Competitor covariates, and interaction term, from stationary models.


```{r tab-2, tab.cap = "(ref:tab-2)"}
regional_stat_coeffs <- rbind(read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_stat_inter_sockeye.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_stat_inter_chum.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_stat_inter_pink.csv")))[,-1] |>
  mutate(Coefficient  = replace_when(Coefficient , Coefficient  == "Comp" ~ "Competitors"))

knitr::kable(regional_stat_coeffs,
             col.names = c("Species", "Ocean Region", "Coefficient", "Lower CI", "Mean", "Upper CI", "Mean % change in R/S"),
             row.names = FALSE,
             align = "lrrcccc",
             booktabs = T,
             longtable=T,
             digits = c(0,0,0,2,2,2,0)) |>
  column_spec(7, width = "2cm")|>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"))
```


(ref:tab-3) Estimated population-specific mean effect sizes for SST and Competitor covariates, and interaction term, from stationary models.


```{r tab-3, tab.cap = "(ref:tab-3)"}
stk_stat_coeffs <- rbind(read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/stk_coefficients_stat_inter_sockeye.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/stk_coefficients_stat_inter_chum.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/stk_coefficients_stat_inter_pink.csv")))[,-1]|>
  mutate(Coefficient  = replace_when(Coefficient , Coefficient  == "Comp" ~ "Competitors"))
knitr::kable(stk_stat_coeffs,
             col.names = c("Species", "Population","Ocean Region", "Coefficient", "Lower CI", "Mean", "Upper CI", "Mean % change in R/S"),
             row.names = FALSE,
             align = "lrrcccc",
             booktabs = T,
             longtable=T,
             digits = c(0,0,0,0,2,2,2,0)) |>
  column_spec(2, width = "3cm") |>
  column_spec(8, width = "2cm")|>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"))
```


(ref:tab-4) Estimated mean effect sizes by ocean region for SST and Competitor covariates, from time-varying 'era' models.


```{r tab-4, tab.cap = "(ref:tab-4)"}

regional_era_coeffs <- rbind(read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_era_sockeye.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_era_chum.csv")),
                              read.csv(here("Rmd/figures/reg_coefficients_era_pink.csv")))[,-7]|>
  mutate(Coefficient  = replace_when(Coefficient , Coefficient  == "Comp" ~ "Competitors")) |>
  filter(!Era == "Stationary" )

knitr::kable(regional_era_coeffs,
             col.names = c("Species", "Ocean Region", "Coefficient", "Era","Lower CI", "Mean", "Upper CI"),
             row.names = FALSE,
             align = "lrrrccc",
             booktabs = T,
             longtable=T,
             digits = c(0,0,0,0,2,2,2))|>
  column_spec(2, width = "3cm") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"))
```


(ref:tab-5) Estimated population-specific mean effect sizes for SST and Competitor covariates, from time-varying 'era' models.


```{r tab-5, tab.cap = "(ref:tab-5)"}

# Literature cited
